catalog_quote: Kham is interpreted as having no function for stress. Watters (2002: 23-4) reports that in bisyllabic and polysyllabic words with monomoraic syllables there is "no discernable stress" but that in trisyllabic forms "there is discernable stress on the final syllable". Elsewhere stress is perceived on final long syllables. These perceptions of stress may be illusory.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only: per Watters 2002 (as summarised by LAPSyD), Takale Kham has no functional word stress; words made of light (monomoraic) syllables show no discernible stress, while trisyllabic words and words ending in a long syllable are perceived with stress on the final syllable. Tone (pitch pattern + voice register) is the contrastive prosody of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: As reported: no discernible stress in bisyllabic/polysyllabic words whose syllables are all monomoraic; discernible stress on the final syllable in trisyllabic forms; stress perceived on final long syllables. LAPSyD adds 'These perceptions of stress may be illusory.'
new_statements.domain_note: Domain as reported: the (phonological) word, by syllable count and syllable weight (monomoraic vs long/CV: syllables). Kham is a word-tone language (two pitch patterns x two voice registers, first-hand in Watters 1971: 42-57); the stress remark is about perceived prominence, which LAPSyD judges functionless and possibly illusory. Watters 1971: 57 notes that CVC and CV: syllables are higher in pitch than CV syllables in polysyllabic stems, which may be the phonetic basis of the 'final long syllable' perception.
new_statements.identity_note: All primary sources describe the Takale (Taka-Sera, Baglung/Rukum) dialect of Kham, i.e. Western Parbate Kham west2420 / kjl (Watters 1971: 2 names the dialect and informant; LAPSyD entry is 'Kham, Takale dialect'; WALS kmh maps to west2420). Wilde 2016, also saved, describes Gamale Kham (gama1251 / kgj), a distinct Glottolog language that is atonal, and says nothing about stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog record's second-hand LAPSyD summary of Watters 2002: 23-24 at the primary wording ('no discernible stress placement' in short open bisyllables; 'discernible stress on the final syllable' in all-short trisyllables; stress on final long syllables; book spells 'discernible', LAPSyD 'discernable') and adds detail LAPSyD omits: stress follows length (a long non-final first syllable takes the stress over the final), stress is stated to be independent of high pitch, and 'usually final long syllable, though there are some exceptions'. Type unchanged: tone language with a predictable, non-contrastive stress statement. Caveat: read from index snippets of the 2002 revision, not fr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Takale Kham is a tone language with non-contrastive, length-driven word stress in polysyllabic morphemes: a long syllable (usually the final one) carries the stress, explicitly 'not to be equated with high pitch'; where all syllables are open and short, bisyllables show no discernible stress placement while trisyllables have stress on the final syllable; where the first syllable is long (rare), stress falls on the long syllable, not the final one. I.e. weight-sensitive with a final default, in a tonal system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the visible snippets
new_statements.exceptions: 'If there is a long syllable somewhere in the string it will usually be the final syllable, though there are some exceptions'; bisyllables with final length+stress are said to derive from old C(r)/C(l) clusters with a schwa first vowel (ex. 16 bəle:-, kəri:-); footnote 6 (content not visible) is attached to the trisyllabic final-stress statement. The LAPSyD clause 'These perceptions of stress may be illusory' does not occur in the book's index (queries 'illusory' returned 0) and looks like Maddieson's own gloss.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Takale (Taka-Sera) dialect of Western Parbate Kham [kjl], west-central Nepal (Rukum), the variety of the catalog record; the held Wilde 2016 paper is Gamale Kham (a different language) and is not evidence for this entry.

tone_statements.quote: Tone in Kham, as with other languages of the Himalayan region, is best described as an inter-section of ‘tonal melody’ and ‘voice register’ (Hale and Pike 1970; Hari 1980). There are two contrastive melodies — a marked, ‘accented’ tone (T1), and an unmarked, ‘neutral’ tone (T2). Voice register has a modifying effect on the fundamental frequencies of tone bearing units, dividing the pitch range into ‘upper’ and ‘lower’ frequencies. ... tone_statements.quote: Tone in Kham, as with many other languages of the Himalayan region, is best described as an intersection of ‘tonal melody’ and ‘voice register.’ There are two contrastive melodies — a marked, ‘accented’ tone, and an unmarked, ‘neutral’ tone. [...] Voice register has a modifying effect on the fundamental frequencies of tone bearing units, dividing the pitch range into ‘upper’ and ‘lower’ frequencies. Thus, lax register, a marked phonation type characterized by breathiness and laryngeal laxity, induces lower frequencies on the syllable than its unmarked counterpart, modal register.

tone.says: Introduction 3.4: tone = intersection of two contrastive 'tonal melodies' (marked/'accented' vs unmarked/'neutral', marked with a tick before the syllable in the Roman orthography) and two 'voice registers' (modal vs lax/breathy, written with post-vocalic h), register dividing the pitch range into upper and lower; lax register is not tied to onset voicing (unlike Bodish) but in some cases to loss of prefixed *s-; melodies not attributable to lost finals; the marked tone probably began as height…
